claims.text: Rapid high-temperature processing followed by rapid quenching promotes formation of a uniform, single-phase noble metal high-entropy alloy rather than phase separation.
The starting noble metal precursor mixture is homogeneous.
Elevated-temperature processing under an inert atmosphere enables atomic intermixing of the constituent metals.
Rapid quenching freezes a disordered alloy structure.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles contain an atomic-scale uniform dispersion of noble metals within the alloy lattice.
Atomic-scale uniform dispersion produces controlled lattice strain and disordered coordination environments around catalytic sites.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution.
Atomic uniformity and associated lattice strain alter the local electronic structure of the noble metals.
The electronic-structure alteration can shift the d-band centers of catalytic sites.
Electronic-structure modulation changes adsorbate binding energies.
Modified adsorbate binding energies lower activation barriers for key catalytic reactions.
Slow cooling promotes phase segregation relative to rapid quenching.
Phase segregation produces less favorable electronic coupling and fewer active sites than a uniform disordered solid solution.
Uniform high-entropy alloy nanoparticles provide more abundant and more active catalytic sites than phase-segregated counterparts.

Under identical catalytic testing conditions, rapidly quenched uniform nanoparticles will exhibit higher conversion efficiency and desired-product selectivity than slowly cooled, phase-segregated alloys.

The proposed relationship is expected to hold for noble metal systems processed under inert atmospheres with controlled high-temperature and quenching conditions, but not necessarily when substantial phase segregation or ordering occurs.
